title: Choose Brink's visual world
question: The roll assigned Intaglio. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: Intaglio
options.thesis: The board is printed like currency: every power is an engraving ink, and ownership is drawn as line-hatching.
options.viewport: The engraved world map fills the screen, each power's land hatched in its ink at its own angle; a quiet side column sets the phase like a serial number above orders, Crisis and Assembly.
options.risk: Tips into an ornate museum piece if guilloche spreads beyond the seals and the Crisis band.

raised.raise: Panels lose their card chrome: state is carried by ink fields and type, never bordered boxes.
The board owns the viewport; during replay one resolved phase fills it at a time.
Centres and tokens are ranked by mark size on a fixed ramp, not by tint.
Panel fields never move between phases; only their values change.

options.label: Wargame Box
options.lineage: 1970s Avalon Hill and SPI boxed wargames, the house that published Diplomacy
options.thesis: Brink as the boxed game it descends from: a printed map sheet, die-cut counters and numbered rule cases.
options.viewport: A flat printed map with square counters stacked in each province, a terrain-key legend and a turn-record track along the top edge.
options.risk: Familiar: it is where most board-game interfaces land, and buff-paper nostalgia can feel dated.

options.label: Guide Map
options.thesis: Provinces become swelling lobes of flat colour divided only by their coastlines; every control is a capsule.
options.viewport: One continent swells across the screen in flat colour lobes, with capsule controls pinned to coastlines.
options.case: Fuses well on clarity, since a map game is a map; loses on audience because it reads playful against straight geopolitics.
options.risk: Cream ground and toy palette undercut the serious half of the brief.

options.label: Manual Tab Board
options.lineage: boxed-software reference manuals with acetate overlays
options.thesis: The rulebook becomes the interface: a stepped tab rail per phase, orders on acetate leaves over a section-hue board.
options.viewport: The map sits under an acetate leaf of orders, with a stepped tab rail for Spring, Fall and Winter down the right edge.
options.case: Holds audience, since board gamers live in rulebooks; weaker on clarity for a screen that must lead with the map.
options.risk: The tab metaphor competes with the map for the first glance.

options.label: Star Atlas
options.thesis: Centres as magnitude-ranked dots on a navy chart.
options.viewport: A navy world chart with centres as ranked dots.
options.case: Fuses poorly: players don't read geopolitics as a night sky, and navy plus one warm accent is a common default.
options.kept: Hierarchy by mark size on a fixed ramp.

options.label: Metro Tiles
options.thesis: Flat tiles and giant cropped lowercase type.
options.viewport: A panorama of tiles; no room for a map.
options.case: Fuses poorly: tiles fight a geographic board and the type has no map to sit on.
options.kept: Chrome deleted: colour fields and type carry state.

options.label: Vertical Feed
options.thesis: One item fills the screen, one snap to the next.
options.case: Fuses poorly: a strategy board needs everything visible at once.

options.label: Split-flap Board
options.viewport: Events as rows on a departure board.
options.case: Fuses poorly: it is an instrument's costume and has nowhere to put the map.
options.kept: Columns never move; only values change.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A clean modern online-Diplomacy board, done at full craft.
canonCard.viewport: A flat political map with a white sidebar of orders and a phase timeline.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from other online Diplomacy sites by design.
